newsitem.title: New zealand: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 4.

text.p: THE DOMINION

The National Party government is searching for ways to attack Labour leader Helen Clark after failing to gain support from economic and financial analysts for its warnings that the election of a centre-left government would mean economic disaster. Despite National's campaign, New Zealand financial markets have held up or firmed in the past couple of months. Overseas investors have been buying heavily into New Zealand government bonds. Page 1.

Former National finance minister Ruth Richardson has hijacked National's election strategy by urging party supporters to vote ACT NZ for a centre-right coalition. She blasted National for "lamentable" campaign tatics and said she could not believe the party was refusing to make deals that could help it stay in power. Page 2.

Former Prime Minister David Lange told an Australian television audience defections by opposition parliamentarians eager for the perks of government could return National to power in New Zealand. Page 2.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger dismissed Labour leader Helen Clark's pledge to set up a poverty commission as he continued to portray the election as a choice between economic growth or stagnation. Clark accused National of trying to hide the "social scandal" of poverty by refusing to monitor the consequences of its policies. Page 2.

Japanese and European investors chasing some of the highest real interest rates in the world have been huge buyers of New Zealand bonds recently while election-shy New Zealand investors are selling out. Market observers say it is the first time since the collapse of DFC in the late 1980s that Japanese investors have returned with large amounts of cash to New Zealand - about $3 billion in the past few weeks. Page 11.

Fund manager Prudential says it has increased its New Zealand holdings in the past three months because inflation and interest rates are heading down and economic growth may be higher next year. Page 11.

Record profits in Wellington-based Steel and Tube's steel distribution and reinforcing divisions were offset by poor results from a new Canadian subsidiary. Steel and Tube reported an 8 percent fall in tax-paid profit to $25.3 million. The acquisition of A J Forsyth last November coincided with earlier than expected cyclical downturn in the British Columbian
forestry industry, causing a severe fall in steel volumes. Page 11.

Independent Newspapers' offer for Wilson and Horton shares through subsidiary Independent Press Communications is fair, according to an independent appraisal by Southpac. The appraisal report says Southpac had assessed the Wilson and Horton shares as being worth between $10.20 and $11.10. Page 11.

More than half of New Zealand's business leaders are not expecting any significant change in economic policy after the election, according to a survey by Ernst and Young and National Business Review. Page 11.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD
Defections by opposition MPs eager for the perks of government could return National to power, former Prime Minister David Lange said on Australia's ABC television. Page 1.

The $10.50 a share takeover bid for Wilson and Horton has been judged fair by an independent appraisal. However, independent directors of the Auckland-based publisher and printer advise shareholders to delay decisions until the directors make a recommendation next week. Page 1.

Flustered Prime Minister Jim Bolger lost his patience briefly with a Radio New Zealand interviewer on Checkpoint as National spent the day trying and failing to shrug off its campaign jinx. Interviewer Neil Billington challenged Bolger to back up his claims that the economy is at risk from a
centre-left government. Bolger found himself rebutting charges that he was trying to talk financial markets into a crisis. "I am the optimist of this campaign." Page 3.

In sharp contrat to the cautious lead-up to other elections, money market interest rates have fallen sharply, the New Zealand dollar has remained at or near eight-year highs and the sharemarket has rebounded from a pre-election fall last week. Overseas factors have been important, clearly outweighing the influence of the election. Page 6.
Former Finance Minister Ruth Richardsoon hijacked National's election strategy by urging party suppporters to vote ACT for a centre-right coalition. Page 6.

Mercury Energy made a fresh offer to WEL Energy yesterday for its pivotal eight percent stake in Power New Zeland. Neither Mercury nor WEL would disclose the price, but it must be above the 800 cents a share which is Mercury's existing offer. Mercury has alkready given 1,000 cents as the upper limit of offers it might make to WEL and the four district councils which control another key stake of seven percent.

Indepedent Newspapers' exchangeable share option is the best deal for Wilson and Horton shareholders, according to Southpac Corporation. In its independent appraisal of the $10.50 a share takeover offer, Southpac places a value up to $11.47 a share on the exhangeable shares alternative, which convert to either cash or Independent Newspaper shares in seven years.

Prudential Portfolio Managers has increased its exposure to New Zealand assets over the past three months, said New Zealand managing director Greg Whitten. "Elections are not something it is sensible to build investment policy around."

Brierley Investments' Thistle Hotels, making its debut on the London Stock Exchange on Wednesday night, might have dropped below its 170 pence issue price without help of its lead broker. Market sources said Merrill Lynch came in to support Thistle as its share price came under pressure.
